Saxenda (liraglutide) injection is a prescription medicine for patients with obesity (BMI ≥30) or overweight (BMI ≥27) who also have weight-related medical problems, to help them lose weight, paired with diet and exercise. Saxenda should not be used with other liraglutide-containing products or other GLP-1s. It is not known if Saxenda is safe and effective when taken with other weight loss products. Saxenda may cause serious side effects including possible thyroid tumors and thyroid cancer. Do not use Saxenda if you or any of your family have ever had a type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or if you have an endocrine system condition called Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Saxenda may cause other serious side effects, including pancreatitis, gallbladder problems, increased risk of low blood sugar, increased heart rate, kidney problems, serious allergic reactions, and depression or suicidal thoughts. #weightloss #loseweight #glp1 #semaglutide #weightlossjourney #healthgoals
Video Transcript: We know that GLP-1 is really effective in helping people who are overweight or obese lose weight. But what does a person actually feel when taking them? It is worth knowing that these drugs work by slowing down stomach emptying and regulating the area of the brain responsible for feelings of satiety and satisfaction. So, one of the sensations is a decrease in appetite, as you feel fuller faster and last longer. One person I interviewed described it as finally understanding what it means to not be hungry all the time. This is very important. Some people report side effects in the first few months of treatment. The most common of these are nausea, abdominal pain , constipation, or diarrhea. This is quite logical, considering that the drug works by slowing down stomach emptying. If food stays in your stomach longer than you're used to, you may feel nauseated or uncomfortable. And if food passes through your stomach more slowly, it makes sense that you might notice changes in your bowel movements. For most people, these symptoms are most noticeable on the day they take the medication or when the dose is increased. Over time, they disappear on their own . In studies of GLP-1, most people reported that they experienced fewer side effects after the first few months of taking it . This is logical, as the usual GLP-1 regimen involves increasing the dose once a month for the first four months. When you reach a dose that you will take long-term, your body knows what to expect and, ideally , adapts, which means less nausea or constipation. So when someone asks you what it's like to take GLP-1, you can say: great.

What can Upneeq do? See the bold, bright difference for yourself. 
Visit ro.co/derm to explore if it's right for you.

Important Safety Information: Upneeq is a prescription eye drop used to treat acquired blepharoptosis (low-lying lids). Ptosis may be a sign of a neurologic or other eye disease. Upneeq should be used with caution if you have heart problems, such as high or low blood pressure, or if you have Sjogren's syndrome. Upneeq may increase the risk of glaucoma if you have untreated narrow-angle glaucoma. For full safety information visit: ro.co/safety-info/upneeq
